title: Linked List Cycle II
description:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return the node where the cycle begins. If there is no cycle, return `null` (`None` in Python).

There is a cycle in a linked list if there is some node in the list that can be reached again by continuously following the `next` pointer. Internally, `pos` is used to denote the 0-indexed position of the node that the tail's `next` pointer connects to (`-1` if there is no cycle). Note that `pos` is not passed as a parameter to `detectCycle`.

Do not modify the linked list. In the examples below, the judge displays the 0-indexed position of the returned node in the original list, or `-1` if `null` is returned.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 10^4].
pos is -1 or a valid index in the linked list.
Do not modify the linked list.
hints: First detect whether a cycle exists using Floyd's slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) pointers.
Suppose the cycle starts `a` steps from `head`, and slow and fast meet `b` steps into a cycle of length `c`. Because fast traveled twice as far as slow, `a + b` is a multiple of `c`.
Reset one pointer to `head` and move both pointers one step at a time; they will meet at the exact entry node of the cycle.

examples.explanation: The tail connects to node index 1 (value 2), so detectCycle returns the node at index 1.
The tail connects to node index 0 (value 1), so detectCycle returns the head node (index 0).
There is no cycle in the linked list, so detectCycle returns null (displayed as -1).
